opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I'd say reasoning is basically when the model has to do some amount of computation at test time to get to the answer, as opposed to just retrieving something it already knows. If you ask a model the capital of France, that's pure recall. It either memorized it during training or it didn't. But if you give it a math problem it hasn't seen before, or a tricky coding task, it can't just look up the answer. It has to combine things it knows, try out different steps, check whether they're working, and build up to a conclusion.

So I'd frame it as reasoning being useful when there's a gap between what's stored in the weights and what the task needs, and you close that gap by thinking at inference time. That's why chain of thought helps so much. You're letting the model use more serial computation than it gets in a single forward pass. A transformer only has so many layers, so there's a limit to how much it can work out in one step. Writing out intermediate steps lets it extend that.

I'd also say a big part of it, which people sometimes underrate, is the error correction side. Good reasoning isn't just going forward step by step. It's noticing "wait, that doesn't look right," backing up, and trying another approach. A lot of what we've seen with training models using RL on reasoning tasks is that they pick up these behaviors. They learn to double-check, consider alternatives, and recover from mistakes, and that's where much of the gain comes from.

So in short, reasoning is doing useful computation at test time, especially the kind that involves search and self-correction, to solve problems you can't answer just from memory.

r001.rationale: The candidate defines reasoning as computation performed at test time and describes combining knowledge through successive steps to reach an answer.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that reasoning is the stuff that requires computation at test time. You can contrast that with knowledge, which is basically retrieval. If I ask you what the capital of France is, you don't have to do any work, you just look it up. But if I give you a math problem, or ask you to figure out how some piece of code is going to behave, there's no way to have memorized the answer, you actually have to do a sequence of steps where each step depends on the result of the previous one. That's reasoning.

And I think that's why chain of thought turned out to be such a big deal for language models. A transformer doing a single forward pass has a fixed amount of compute per token, so there's a hard ceiling on how much sequential computation it can do before it has to commit to an answer. When you let the model write out intermediate steps, you're giving it a scratchpad, and now the amount of computation scales with the length of the output rather than being fixed by the depth of the network. So in some sense, the model "reasoning" just means it's spending more tokens, and therefore more compute, on a problem that needs it.

There's also a second piece, which I think is maybe underrated, which is that reasoning involves some kind of search or self-correction. It's not just linear deduction. If you watch a good mathematician work, they try an approach, notice it's not going anywhere, back up, and try something else. A lot of what we've been doing with RL on these models is trying to get them to do that well, to recognize when they've made a mistake and recover from it, rather than just confidently plowing ahead. So I'd say reasoning at test time is deliberately spending compute, doing sequential steps, and being able to check your own work along the way.

r001.rationale: The candidate defines reasoning as requiring computation at test time and explains that it involves sequential steps, each depending on the previous one.

astra-6.text:
I’d define it as using computation at test time to work out an answer that you can’t produce in one immediate step. Instead of just recognizing a pattern and giving a response, the model does some intermediate work—breaks the problem into pieces, derives something, maybe checks it—and uses that work to arrive at an answer.

It’s not a sharp distinction, because something that requires reasoning for one model might be an immediate response for another. But the operational question is: can the model use more computation at test time to get a better answer, with its weights held fixed?

r001.rationale: Defines reasoning as using computation at test time and describes intermediate steps such as breaking down or deriving an answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d say reasoning is when the model needs to do some intermediate computation to arrive at an answer, rather than just producing an answer it already knows. It might need to break a problem into steps, work through those steps, and check whether they fit together.

At test time, that means there’s something useful for the model to do with additional computation. Instead of immediately committing to an answer, it can explore an approach, notice that it doesn’t work, and try something else. Of course, the boundary is fuzzy, because even producing an immediate answer involves computation. But that’s roughly the distinction I have in mind.

r001.rationale: Defines reasoning as intermediate computation and describes working through steps using additional computation at test time.
